title: Photosynthesis & Plant Nutrition
description: How plants use light energy to make glucose — the equation, leaf structure, limiting factors, mineral nutrition, and how to test for starch.

notes.heading: The Photosynthesis Equation
notes.body: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants (and some algae and bacteria) convert light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. The word equation: Carbon Dioxide + Water → Glucose + Oxygen. The balanced chemical equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Light energy (absorbed by chlorophyll) is essential — it powers the reaction. Photosynthesis takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells, primarily in the leaves. The raw materials come from: CO₂ diffuses in from the air through stomata; water is absorbed from the soil through roots and transported via xylem vessels. The products: glucose is used for energy, growth, and storage; oxygen is released as a by-product through the stomata.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing carbon dioxide and water entering a chloroplast, powered by light energy, to produce glucose and oxygen.
illustration.caption: Light energy absorbed by chlorophyll drives the conversion of CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen.

notes.heading: Leaf Structure and Adaptations for Photosynthesis
notes.body: A leaf is a highly adapted organ for photosynthesis. From top to bottom: (1) Waxy cuticle — transparent waterproof layer preventing water loss. (2) Upper epidermis — single layer of transparent cells letting light through. (3) Palisade mesophyll — tightly packed columnar cells near the top of the leaf, packed with chloroplasts to absorb maximum light. This is the main photosynthetic tissue. (4) Spongy mesophyll — loosely packed cells with air spaces for gas exchange (CO₂ in, O₂ out). (5) Lower epidermis — contains most stomata (pores) surrounded by guard cells. Stomata open during the day for gas exchange and close at night to reduce water loss. (6) Vascular bundles (veins) — contain xylem (water up from roots) and phloem (sugars away to the rest of the plant). Key adaptations: large surface area, thin structure (short diffusion distance), transparent epidermis, air spaces, and extensive vein network.

illustration.alt: Cross-section of a leaf showing cuticle, epidermis, palisade and spongy mesophyll, stomata, and vein.
illustration.caption: CO₂ enters through stomata and reaches the photosynthetic palisade mesophyll.

notes.heading: Limiting Factors of Photosynthesis
notes.body: A limiting factor is any factor that restricts the rate of a process when in short supply. For photosynthesis, there are three main limiting factors: (1) Light intensity — as light increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases proportionally at first. Beyond a certain point, the rate plateaus because another factor becomes limiting. (2) Carbon dioxide concentration — similar pattern to light. Normal atmospheric CO₂ is about 0.04%; increasing this boosts photosynthesis until another factor limits it. (3) Temperature — rate increases with temperature as enzymes work faster, but above about 40-45°C, enzymes denature and the rate drops sharply to zero. Important: at any given moment, only one factor is truly limiting the rate. If you increase a non-limiting factor, nothing changes. Graph interpretation: a plateau means that factor is no longer limiting — something else is. To identify which factor, raise one variable at a time and observe whether the rate changes.

illustration.alt: Graph showing rate of photosynthesis rising with light intensity then plateauing as another factor becomes limiting.
illustration.caption: Once a factor is no longer limiting, the curve plateaus until another variable is increased.

notes.heading: Uses of Glucose in Plants
notes.body: Plants produce glucose through photosynthesis but do not store glucose directly (it is too reactive and soluble). Instead, glucose is converted and used in five main ways: (1) Respiration — glucose is broken down in mitochondria to release ATP energy for cell activities. (2) Starch — glucose molecules are linked into long chains of starch, an insoluble polysaccharide stored in leaves, stems, and storage organs (e.g., potatoes). Starch is ideal for storage because it is compact and insoluble (doesn't affect water balance of cells). (3) Cellulose — glucose converted into cellulose fibres to build and strengthen cell walls, especially in growing tissues. (4) Proteins — glucose combined with nitrate ions (absorbed from soil) to make amino acids, which are assembled into proteins for growth and enzymes. (5) Lipids (fats and oils) — glucose converted into lipids for cell membranes and as an energy store in seeds. Nitrates and magnesium ions are essential inputs alongside glucose.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing glucose branching into five uses: respiration, starch, cellulose, proteins, and lipids.
illustration.caption: Glucose from photosynthesis is converted into energy, storage molecules, and structural materials.

notes.heading: Mineral Nutrition and Deficiency Symptoms
notes.body: Plants need mineral ions absorbed from the soil for healthy growth. The three most important are: (1) Nitrates (NO₃⁻) — needed to make amino acids and proteins for growth. Deficiency: stunted growth, yellow older leaves. (2) Magnesium ions (Mg²⁺) — central atom in the chlorophyll molecule; essential for photosynthesis. Deficiency: yellowing between leaf veins (chlorosis), starting with older leaves. (3) Potassium ions (K⁺) — helps enzyme activity and regulates stomatal opening/closing. Deficiency: yellow leaf edges, poor flower/fruit development. Other minerals: Phosphates (PO₄³⁻) for DNA and ATP; calcium for cell wall structure. Farmers and gardeners use fertilisers (NPK — Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium) to replace minerals removed by harvesting crops. Organic fertilisers (manure, compost) release nutrients slowly. In hydroponics, plants grow in mineral solution without soil — this proves soil itself is not essential, only the minerals and water it provides.

illustration.alt: Diagram showing roots absorbing nitrate, magnesium, and potassium ions from soil, with leaves displaying each deficiency symptom.
illustration.caption: Nitrates, magnesium, and potassium are taken up by roots; deficiencies produce distinctive leaf symptoms.

notes.heading: Testing a Leaf for Starch — Practical
notes.body: This experiment tests whether photosynthesis has occurred (starch is only produced by photosynthesis). Method: (1) Place the leaf in boiling water for 1-2 minutes — this kills the leaf and stops all chemical reactions. (2) Turn off the Bunsen burner (ethanol is highly flammable!). (3) Transfer the leaf to a test tube of ethanol and place the tube in the hot water bath. The ethanol boils and removes chlorophyll, decolourising the leaf. (4) Remove the leaf and rinse in cold water to soften it. (5) Spread the leaf on a white tile and add a few drops of iodine solution. Result: Blue-black colour = starch present (photosynthesis occurred). Yellow-brown (no change) = no starch (no photosynthesis). Safety: ethanol is flammable — always use a water bath, never heat directly over a flame. This test is commonly used to investigate whether light, CO₂, or chlorophyll are necessary for photosynthesis.

illustration.alt: Four-step diagram for testing a leaf for starch: boiling water, ethanol bath, rinsing, and iodine test.
illustration.caption: A leaf is boiled, decolourised in ethanol, rinsed, and then tested with iodine; blue-black indicates starch.

notes.heading: Investigating the Rate of Photosynthesis
notes.body: The classic practical uses pondweed (e.g., Elodea or Cabomba) to measure oxygen production: (1) Place pondweed in a beaker of water with a lamp at a measured distance. (2) Add sodium hydrogen carbonate to the water to ensure CO₂ is not limiting. (3) Count the number of oxygen bubbles released per minute, or collect the gas in an inverted measuring cylinder. (4) Vary one factor: light intensity (by changing lamp distance), CO₂ concentration (by varying sodium hydrogen carbonate), or temperature (using a water bath). Controlled variables: type of pondweed, length of cutting, volume of water, time allowed for equilibration. Key relationship: rate of photosynthesis ∝ 1 ÷ (distance from lamp)² — this is the inverse square law. As you double the distance, light intensity falls to one quarter. Plot rate vs light intensity for the characteristic curve (linear rise → plateau).

illustration.alt: Diagram of the pondweed photosynthesis experiment with a lamp, beaker, bubbles, and a rate versus light intensity graph.
illustration.caption: Counting oxygen bubbles from pondweed shows how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis.

flashcards.definition: The process by which green plants use light energy to convert CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen.
flashcards.example: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, catalysed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts.

flashcards.definition: The green pigment found in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light best; green light is reflected, making leaves appear green.

flashcards.definition: A variable that restricts the rate of a process when it is in short supply.
flashcards.example: On a cloudy day, light intensity limits photosynthesis; adding CO₂ will not increase the rate.

flashcards.definition: An insoluble polysaccharide made by linking glucose molecules; the main storage form of carbohydrate in plants.
flashcards.example: Excess glucose from photosynthesis is stored as starch grains in chloroplasts.

flashcards.definition: Tiny pores, mainly on the underside of leaves, through which CO₂ enters and O₂ and water vapour exit.
flashcards.example: Guard cells control the opening and closing of each stoma.

flashcards.definition: The main photosynthetic tissue in leaves — column-shaped cells packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface.
flashcards.example: Palisade cells absorb the most light because they are positioned directly below the transparent upper epidermis.

flashcards.definition: A pair of kidney-shaped cells surrounding each stoma; they swell (turgid) to open or shrink (flaccid) to close the pore.
flashcards.example: Guard cells open stomata during the day to allow gas exchange and close them at night to conserve water.

flashcards.definition: Dead, hollow tubes reinforced with lignin that transport water and dissolved minerals from roots up to the leaves.
flashcards.example: Water moves up through xylem in the transpiration stream, supplying photosynthesis.

flashcards.definition: Living tubes that transport dissolved sugars (translocation) from leaves to other parts of the plant for use or storage.
flashcards.example: Glucose produced in photosynthesis is transported by phloem to roots, fruits, and growing tips.

flashcards.definition: Mineral ions absorbed from soil, needed by plants to make amino acids and proteins for growth.
flashcards.example: A plant deficient in nitrates will show stunted growth and yellowing of older leaves.

flashcards.definition: Mineral absorbed from soil; the central atom of each chlorophyll molecule. Essential for photosynthesis.
flashcards.example: Without magnesium, plants cannot make chlorophyll; leaves turn yellow (chlorosis) and photosynthesis slows.

flashcards.definition: Iodine solution turns from yellow-brown to blue-black in the presence of starch, indicating photosynthesis occurred.
flashcards.example: A leaf boiled in ethanol and then tested with iodine will show blue-black patches where starch is present.

questions.stem: What are the reactants (raw materials) for photosynthesis?
choices: Glucose and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and water
Glucose and carbon dioxide
Water and oxygen
questions.explanation: CO₂ (from the air through stomata) and water (from the soil through roots) are the raw materials for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: In which organelle does photosynthesis occur?
choices: Mitochondria
Nucleus
Ribosome
Chloroplast
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain the green pigment chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy to power photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A plant kept in total darkness for 24 hours will:
choices: Speed up photosynthesis to compensate
Stop photosynthesis completely — no light means no reaction
Continue photosynthesising at a reduced rate
Switch to photosynthesising using stored starch
questions.explanation: Light is an essential requirement. Without light, the light-dependent reactions cannot occur, so photosynthesis stops entirely.

questions.stem: Why do plants convert glucose into starch for storage?
choices: Starch releases more energy than glucose
Starch is insoluble so it does not affect the cell's water balance by osmosis
Starch is easier to transport through phloem
Glucose is toxic to plant cells in high concentrations
questions.explanation: Glucose is soluble and would increase the cell's solute concentration, drawing in excess water by osmosis. Starch is insoluble and compact — ideal for storage.

questions.stem: Which gas is released as a by-product of photosynthesis?
choices: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Oxygen
Hydrogen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released when water molecules are split (photolysis) during the light-dependent reactions.

questions.stem: A student is using pondweed to measure photosynthesis rate. The lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm away. What happens to the rate of photosynthesis?
choices: It doubles
It stays the same — light is not a limiting factor
It decreases to roughly one quarter of the original rate
It decreases by half
questions.explanation: Light intensity follows the inverse square law. Doubling the distance means the light intensity falls to 1/(2²) = 1/4, so the rate drops to roughly one quarter (provided light is the limiting factor).

questions.stem: In the starch test practical, why is the leaf boiled in ethanol?
choices: To kill the leaf and stop enzyme reactions
To remove chlorophyll so the colour change with iodine is visible
To extract glucose so only starch remains
To sterilise the leaf for safe handling
questions.explanation: Ethanol removes (extracts) the green chlorophyll, decolourising the leaf. This means the blue-black iodine result is clearly visible against a pale leaf.

questions.stem: A plant shows yellowing of older leaves and stunted growth. Which mineral deficiency is most likely?
choices: Potassium
Magnesium
Nitrate
Phosphate
questions.explanation: Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth (can't make proteins) and yellowing of older leaves as nitrogen is mobilised to new growth.

questions.stem: Which leaf tissue is the main site of photosynthesis?
choices: Upper epidermis
Spongy mesophyll
Palisade mesophyll
Xylem
questions.explanation: Palisade mesophyll cells are tightly packed near the top of the leaf and contain the highest concentration of chloroplasts.

questions.stem: A greenhouse grower increases CO₂ concentration but sees no rise in photosynthesis rate. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The plants have stopped respiring
Another factor (e.g., light or temperature) is now the limiting factor
Plants do not respond to additional CO₂
The stomata have permanently closed
questions.explanation: When increasing one factor does not raise the rate, that factor is no longer limiting — something else (like light intensity or temperature) is restricting photosynthesis instead.

questions.stem: During a hot, dry day, a plant closes its stomata to reduce water loss. What is the immediate effect on photosynthesis?
choices: Photosynthesis speeds up because water is conserved
Photosynthesis slows down because CO₂ cannot enter the leaf
No effect — photosynthesis continues normally
Photosynthesis switches to using oxygen instead of CO₂
questions.explanation: If stomata are closed, CO₂ cannot diffuse into the leaf. With no CO₂, the light-independent reactions cannot proceed, and photosynthesis slows or stops.

questions.stem: Why must the iodine test for starch be done on a leaf that has been boiled and decolourised?
choices: Raw leaves react dangerously with iodine
The waxy cuticle and chlorophyll would prevent the iodine from reaching and reacting with starch inside the cells
Boiling converts glucose into starch so it can be detected
Iodine only works on dead tissue
questions.explanation: Boiling breaks down cell membranes (making cells permeable), and ethanol removes the waxy cuticle and chlorophyll, allowing iodine to penetrate and react with starch.

questions.stem: Why does a leaf from a variegated plant (one with green and white sections) produce starch only in the green areas?
choices: The white areas are dead tissue
Only the green areas contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll, so only those areas can photosynthesise
The white areas have thicker cuticles blocking CO₂
Starch is transported away from the white areas
questions.explanation: The white areas lack chlorophyll. Without chlorophyll, light energy cannot be absorbed and photosynthesis cannot occur — so no glucose, and therefore no starch, is produced there.

questions.stem: Which gas is needed by plants to combine with glucose to make amino acids and proteins?
choices: Oxygen from photosynthesis
Nitrogen from nitrates absorbed by roots
Carbon dioxide from the air
Hydrogen from water
questions.explanation: Plants combine glucose with nitrate ions (containing nitrogen) from the soil to synthesise amino acids, which are then assembled into proteins.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a destarched plant has one leaf sealed in a flask with soda lime (absorbs CO₂) and another leaf sealed with normal air. After 24 hours of light, which leaf will test positive for starch?
choices: Both leaves — light is the only requirement
Neither leaf — sealing them stops photosynthesis
Only the leaf with normal air — CO₂ is necessary for photosynthesis
Only the leaf with soda lime — CO₂ inhibits starch production
questions.explanation: Soda lime absorbs CO₂, so the leaf in that flask has no CO₂ available. Without CO₂, photosynthesis cannot occur and no starch is produced. The leaf with normal air (which contains CO₂) can photosynthesise and produce starch.
